themes.name: Rabbit Holes Worth Falling Down
themes.tagline: One obscure question, one satisfying answer, and a brain slightly more interesting than before.

items.title: Who Said The First Bad Word On The Moon?
items.why_watch: A perfectly sized two-minute detour into a genuinely obscure historical footnote: who broke decorum first on the lunar surface. Vsauce treats it as a mini-mystery with a satisfying answer, and the constraint of the short format keeps it tight and fun.

items.title: Why is the speed of light 299,792,458 m/s? (and not 300,000 km/s)
items.description:
To try everything Brilliant has to offer—free—for a full 30 days, visit https://brilliant.org/FloatHeadPhysics . You’ll also get 20% off an annual premium subscription

Let's explore how the speed of light in vacuum is connected to the size of the earth!

This video was sponsored by Brilliant
items.why_watch: The specific question here is sharper than it first appears: the speed of light is a defined constant, so why isn't it a round number? The answer ties the meter's historical definition to the size of the Earth, and the chain of reasoning is genuinely satisfying rather than trivia-level. A nice 16-minute reminder that unit systems carry hidden history.

themes.name: Where Physics Gets Weird
themes.tagline: The universe doesn't play by tidy rules — and these videos show exactly where the seams start to split.

items.title: Why Quantum Gravity Doesn't Work
items.description:
Try Opera Browser for free: https://opr.as/Opera-browser-physicsexplainedvideos

Quantum mechanics and general relativity both describe nature with astonishing precision, but when we try to combine them using the same perturbative tools that work so well in quantum electrodynamics, the method breaks down.

In QED, the small value of the fine-structure constant ensures that higher-order corrections remain tiny, allowing us to make incredibly accurate predictions. For gravity, however, the effecti
items.why_watch: This video pinpoints exactly why combining quantum mechanics and general relativity fails — not hand-waving about 'incompatibility,' but a precise explanation of why the perturbative math that works beautifully in QED produces unmanageable infinities when gravity enters the picture. At 29 minutes it's genuinely technical, but Physics Explained earns the runtime by building the argument step by step rather than retreating into metaphor.

items.title: The River Model of General Relativity
items.description:
Does space "flow" like a river? There's an analogy in General Relativity positing exactly that, and which, astonishingly enough, conveys the sophistication of Einstein's theory via a few simple intuitions. But how truthful is such a view, and what would it imply about the most infamous of massive objects to inhabit our universe -- that of the black hole? Climb aboard our river-boat and find out! Plus -- Curious Edgar finds himself in more than one vertiginous predicament.

Credit for the thumbna
items.why_watch: The 'river model' of spacetime — where space itself flows inward toward a black hole like a current — is one of the more underexplored analogies in pop-physics, and Dialect takes it seriously enough to examine where it holds up and where it quietly breaks down. The black hole section alone makes it worth the 20 minutes, especially if Schwarzschild coordinates have ever left you cold.

themes.name: The Signal Behind the Static
themes.tagline: Electrons, gaps, and the elegant logic hiding inside your circuit board.

items.title: From capacitor to passive filters - impedance, reactance and high order filter issues
items.description:
This video talks about passive filters starting from the inner properties of capacitors to high order filters. We explains why current flows in a circuit although the presence of the capacitor and why this foundamental element is used to create filters allowing only some frequencies to pass. We approch filters of second order and the problem you face in building filter of high order. 
Miller effect made easy: https://youtu.be/TD3jhSzOdqI
Differential Amplifier : https://youtu.be/bongv60GqIY
items.why_watch: A compact electronics primer that traces a clean line from capacitor fundamentals — why current flows despite the gap — through to the real-world headaches of building high-order passive filters, including the Miller effect. Worth bookmarking if you've ever followed a filter design tutorial without understanding why it actually works.

morning_soundtrack.title: Just Penelope – “Copenhagen”
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Just Penelope's debut EP Great Lake is out this Friday, and they're still heightening the anticipation. The Bloomington band has shared " After " (which made our list of the 5 best songs of the week ) and " Sister ," but the latest single "Copenhagen" might be the best one yet.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: The kind of song that makes you want to book a flight somewhere cold and beautiful just to feel something.

morning_soundtrack.title: Song People – “The Cone”
morning_soundtrack.snippet: They call themselves Song People, and they're once again proving it today. The Philly band showed off their unique blend of jangle-pop, dream-pop, post-punk, and folk on " Silver Flag ," the lead single from new album Tho I Seem Tame . Second single "The Cone" is out now, and it continues to make me imagine a timeline in which Fairport Convention were a C86 band.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Autumnal jangle that sounds like flipping through a dog-eared paperback at a record fair in the drizzle.

morning_soundtrack.title: Caroline Rose – “Calm” & “Hello Again, Jim”
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Gentling The Horse At The Walt Whitman Mall is going to be a trip. Caroline Rose has previewed the forthcoming album with bizarro bangers " Yip Yip Yow " and " Chow Mein ," and now she's sharing "Calm" and "Hello Again, Jim."
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Delightfully unhinged art-pop for people who take their weirdness very seriously and their seriousness not at all.

morning_soundtrack.title: CROWDFUNDING RADAR: Amber WEsterman, Tuatha Dea, Hitch & The Giddyup
morning_soundtrack.snippet: This month's crowdfunding radar rounds up three worthy campaigns with streaming at the core of their asks.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: The warm, communal energy of passing a hat around a folk festival campfire for artists who still believe music is worth fighting for.

morning_soundtrack.title: Porridge Radio’s Dana Margolin Launches Debut Solo Single
morning_soundtrack.snippet: The Brighton four-piece announced their breakup last year
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: The bittersweet clarity of stepping out of a band's shadow and into your own uncertain, quietly electric morning.

morning_soundtrack.title: M83, O Slow, Angela Autumn, and More: This Week’s Pitchfork Selects Playlist
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Our weekly playlist highlights songs that our writers, editors, and contributors are listening to on repeat
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: A curated sonic mood board for the week's most restless, searching ears.

morning_soundtrack.title: I Will Die In This Jean Jacket :: Hang From A Cloud
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Minneapolis lifer Jim Blaha goes it alone on Hang From A Cloud, a raw, bedroom-recorded set of wistful garage-psych and punk songs that crackle with romantic desperation. From the breathy “Some New Day” to the furious, sotto voce anthems of “D.O.A.,” Blaha distills decades in the underground into something intimate, ferocious, and beautifully unvarnished. The post I Will Die In This Jean Jacket :: Hang From A Cloud first appeared on Aquarium Drunkard .
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Late-night bedroom recordings that feel like a love letter written in shaky handwriting to no one and everyone at once.

morning_soundtrack.title: The Heartbreakers Reunite Alongside Chris Stapleton at Americana Awards: Watch
morning_soundtrack.snippet: They performed "American Girl," "Breakdown," and "You Wreck Me." The Heartbreakers Reunite Alongside Chris Stapleton at Americana Awards: Watch Alex Krinsky
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: The chest-swelling warmth of an encore nobody knew they needed until the first chord hit and the room remembered who they were.

morning_soundtrack.title: Is Burt Bacharach Jazz? Clarinetist Adrian Galante, vocalist John Pagano and writer Will Friedwald Answer in the Affirmative with Going Bacharach
morning_soundtrack.snippet: I f you walk past the 150-seat Marjorie S. Deane Little Theater on West 64th Street in New York, you’ll hear the humming, thrumming sound …
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Velvet-curtained and candlelit, like a supper club where the cocktails arrive just as the melody you've always known finally makes sense.

morning_soundtrack.title: Drummer Matt Wilson’s Good Trouble Fight Power with Love
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Jazz drummer Matt Wilson's political outrage and resistance are present but come through an embrace of love, community, and gorgeous music.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Political fire wrapped in a bear hug — the sound of resistance that somehow still makes you want to dance with a stranger.

morning_soundtrack.title: Wesley Stace Settles into a Stylish Vibe on ‘One Last Heist’
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Prolific singer-songwriter Wesley Stace continues to mine a delightful jazz-lounge groove on his latest beguiling record, One Last Heist .
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: The sophisticated ease of a slow gin martini at a corner table, unhurried and entirely sure of itself.

morning_soundtrack.title: Matt B Goes Home and Lets the Ocean Do the Talking
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Matt B's ALKEBULAN III opens at a door in Ghana and ends with the Atlantic given a speaking voice. In between is the sound of a man learning a language his family had taken from them.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: A deeply personal homecoming unfolding like tide — patient, ancestral, and carrying the weight of everything the water once swallowed.

global_silver_linings.title: Good News in History September 17
global_silver_linings.snippet: Happy 41st birthday to The Great 8, Alexander Ovechkin. Playing left wing for the Washington Capitals since 2004, he is quite simply among the greatest goal scorers in the history of ice hockey. He has won the Hart Memorial Trophy for Most Valuable Player three times (in 2008, 2009, and 2013), the Lester B. Pearson Award […]
global_silver_linings.reason: Looking back at history's bright moments reminds us that humans have always found ways to solve problems, show courage, and make the world better — and that thread continues today.

global_silver_linings.title: Millennials hilariously dissect why they made ‘duckface’ a thing in early 2000s photos
global_silver_linings.reason: There's something quietly joyful about a generation laughing collectively at its own awkward past — shared self-awareness like this is the glue that keeps communities feeling human and connected.

global_silver_linings.title: 8 low-cost hobbies that add hours of joy to your week
global_silver_linings.snippet: Image alt text: Hands carefully pressing colorful flowers between the pages of an open book on a wooden table surrounded by dried botanicals and greenery Research has put a number on the value of a good hobby: eight hours. That is how much joy, defined as deep satisfaction, gratification, and accomplishment, studies suggest a person […] The post 8 low-cost hobbies that add hours of joy to your week first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .
global_silver_linings.reason: Joy doesn't have to be expensive, and rediscovering simple hobbies — whether it's growing something, making something, or learning something new — is a powerful reminder that a richer life is within almost everyone's reach.

discovery_articles.title: The Academy of Natural Sciences in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania
discovery_articles.snippet: The Academy of Natural Sciences is the oldest natural history museum in the country (and the Americas). It has everything the curious could hope for -- dinosaurs, ancient fish and birds, an emphasis on conservation, and a deep-seated appreciation for the natural world. Although many of the subjects have been in the museum for well over a century (the academy first opened its doors in 1812), they are well preserved, and their exhibits carefully crafted with hand painted scenes in the background.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: The oldest natural history museum in the Americas opened its doors in 1812 — when Napoleon was still a present tense problem and the word 'dinosaur' hadn't even been coined yet. Whatever curiosity built this place was ahead of its time in the most quietly magnificent way.

discovery_articles.title: A 66-Million-Year-Old Feather Trapped in Dinosaur Poop Might Help Explain Why Some Birds Survived Mass Extinction
discovery_articles.snippet: Discovered in Montana in 2016, the cherry-size coprolite contains feathers, bones and evidence of the bird's last meal before the creature was eaten by a theropod
discovery_articles.ferns_note: A feather preserved inside dinosaur excrement for 66 million years is the most undignified — and illuminating — fossil imaginable, offering a snapshot of predator, prey, and last meal in a single cherry-sized time capsule. The bird that became lunch may hold clues to why its relatives survived an extinction that ended the world as it was.

discovery_articles.title: Some Fish in the Great Lakes Might Be More Than 400 Years Old, a Study Suggests, Outliving Around 15 Generations of Humans
discovery_articles.snippet: Lake sturgeon may be among the longest-living vertebrates, second only to Greenland sharks, according to recent research. However, scientists note that follow-up work is necessary to clarify the species’ lifespan
discovery_articles.ferns_note: There may be lake sturgeon quietly gliding through the Great Lakes right now that were already old when the Mayflower crossed the Atlantic — living through 15 human generations without once being asked their opinion on any of it. Second only to Greenland sharks in longevity, they are the patient, silver elders of freshwater.

discovery_articles.title: Tasmanian Devils Lived Alongside Humans in Northwestern Australia as Far Back as 45,000 Years Ago, Researchers Find
discovery_articles.snippet: Fossils and marked bones unearthed in a Juukan Gorge cave suggest that the marsupial species not only once lived in the region but may have been a “garbage compactor on four legs” for its human population
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Tasmanian devils — now clinging to existence on a single island — once roamed northwestern Australia alongside humans 45,000 years ago, apparently serving as the neighborhood's unofficial waste management. The marked bones suggest people knew exactly what these creatures were useful for, which is a strangely tender detail about a very ancient coexistence.

discovery_articles.title: Art by Humans, For Humans: A Letter from Our Editorial Director
discovery_articles.snippet: Art is an act of faith in a world that can make hope feel impossible.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: In a single quiet line — 'art is an act of faith in a world that can make hope feel impossible' — an editorial director says the thing most manifestos spend a thousand words failing to land. Sometimes the most radical curatorial statement is just telling the truth.

featured_read.title: Terminal lucidity: when dying dementia patients regain awareness
featured_read.snippet: The reports span centuries and cultures. If they’re real, memory and identity might be far more recoverable than we thought - by Ariel Zeleznikow-Johnston Read on Psyche
featured_read.blurb: Across centuries and cultures, people with advanced dementia have returned to full clarity in their final hours — and if these accounts hold up, they quietly upend everything we think we know about where the self goes when memory dissolves. This is the piece to read slowly, in a quiet room.

reading_room.title: On the “Chattanooga Choo Choo”
reading_room.snippet: “Lately, though, I have become fascinated by the so-called big bands on the SiriusXM station called ‘40s Junction.’ ”
reading_room.blurb: A writer falls unexpectedly under the spell of big-band radio and finds, in the swinging geometry of the Chattanooga Choo Choo, a small argument for why certain music refuses to stay in the past. Consider this your permission to linger somewhere unhurried.

reading_room.title: A True-Crime Producer Posed as an Heiress — Then Allegedly Stole $30 Million
reading_room.snippet: "Mary Carole McDonnell made low-budget crime shows, but her own story was built on deceptions fit for one of her series. Now, she’s on the FBI’s Most Wanted list and the target of a global manhunt."
reading_room.blurb: Mary Carole McDonnell spent her career packaging other people's criminal audacity into tidy television narratives — until she apparently decided to live inside one herself, to the tune of thirty million dollars. The irony is almost too neat to be real, and yet here we are.

reading_room.title: “Simple Recipes”
reading_room.snippet: There is a simple recipe for making rice. My father taught it to me when I was a child. Back then, I used to sit up on the kitchen counter watching him, how he sifted the grains in his hands,
reading_room.blurb: A bowl of rice becomes the quiet container for everything a father passes to a child without saying so directly — love, ritual, the particular weight of cultural inheritance. Madeleine Thien writes about cooking the way other people write about grief, because she understands they are often the same thing.

reading_room.title: Destroying Humanity Is Against the Law
reading_room.snippet: Don’t wait for a mass-extinction event before holding AI developers accountable.
reading_room.blurb: The argument here is bracingly simple: if we have laws against mass harm, why are they not being applied to the people building systems capable of it? This is the essay that will make you want to call your representative, or at least your lawyer.

reading_room.title: What Comes After America
reading_room.snippet: Emily St. John Mandel’s latest work of science fiction considers the tenuousness of any possible future.
reading_room.blurb: Emily St. John Mandel has made a habit of imagining futures that feel more like warnings than predictions, and her latest asks the question that hums beneath all of them: what exactly are we trying to preserve, and for whom? A good one to sit with as the news does what the news does.

garden_note.note: There's a particular quality to early-autumn mornings in Zürich — the air carries that first real chill, and the dahlias in the border are suddenly the bravest things in the garden, blazing away while the maples hint at what's coming. Step outside around first light at 06:35 and you'll find the cobwebs jewelled with dew, every strand catching the pale gold that precedes sunrise.

Sowing lamb's lettuce (Feldsalat) for autumn and winter salads
Raking and composting early fallen leaves

news.blurb: If you've ever wanted cookware with Ramsay's seal of approval, this debut bakeware set sounds like the kind of splurge that quietly earns its place in your kitchen.

news.title: Hoy Is Bringing Night-Market Energy to NYC
news.snippet: This excerpt was originally published in Pre Shift, our newsletter for the hospitality industry. Subscribe for more first-person accounts, advice, and interviews. This is the first installment of our series Getting on the Map, presented by Apple Maps.
news.blurb: NYC's night-market scene just got a compelling new chapter, and Hoy sounds like exactly the kind of electric, lived-in dining experience worth following closely.

news.title: How to turn excess olive brine into a lipsmacking salad dressing – recipe
news.snippet: The liquid from a jar of olives is naturally chock-full of savoury flavour, so why should it go to waste? It’s perfect for sprucing up a salad Olive brine is a simple byproduct that has so much flavour, and it elevates a classic salade nicoise dressing while keeping things colourful, elegant and relatively simple.
news.blurb: A gentle reminder that the brine pooling at the bottom of your olive jar is essentially free umami — and this piece makes a convincing case for never pouring it down the drain again.

recipe.title: Affogato
recipe.snippet: Margot Lecarpentier is one of the best bartenders in Paris. At her bar, Combat, she shakes and stirs up cocktails – with and without alcohol – that are some of the best in the city. One a warm summer day, Margot stopped by to make an Affogato for us to enjoy in my backyard.
recipe.blurb: An affogato is one of summer's most effortless pleasures — just a shot of espresso and good ice cream — and with a Paris bartender's touch guiding you, it feels like the most elegant thing you'll make all season.

larder.seasonal_note: Zürich's Tuesday and Saturday Bürkliplatz market is flush with Zwetschgen right now — those dark, oblong Italian prune plums that beg to be halved and pressed into a buttery Zwetschgenwähe, the pastry filling your kitchen with the kind of spiced, jammy warmth that makes an early autumn morning feel entirely intentional.

fern_data.greeting: Monday has the nerve to arrive anyway. Worth meeting it with the question of who swore first on the moon, a fish in Lake Superior that has outlived fifteen human generations, and the uncomfortable news that quantum gravity simply doesn't work.
